the LAGEOS-type satellite in critical supplementary orbit (CSOC) concept is a very powerful tool for testing general relativity, in particular for measuring the Lense-Thiring effect.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of the Lense-Thiring effect in the Earth gravitational field by analysing a pair of LAGEOSType satellites in critical supplementary orbital configuration.
the detection and measurement of the LTT with an accuracy level better than 1% by means of the LAGEOS-type CSOC satellites.
the development and implementation of a new, highly sensitive space test of the Lense-Thiirring effect, based on the use of a new pair of LAGOS-type satellites in CSOC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, with the new pair of LEO satellites in CSOC, the Lense– Thirring effect could be detected at the 3σ level with an accuracy of 0.5% and at the 2σ level with an 0.3% accuracy level.
the Lense– Thirring detection is possible with a new pair of LAGOS-type satellites in CSOC, but it is still not a certainty.
the Lense-Thirling effect could be measured with an accuracy level less than 1% by using a pair of LAGEOSTYPE satellites in CSOC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Lense– Thirring effect detection by means of a pair of LAGEOs in CSOC configuration is feasible and that the forthcoming, new high-quality gravity models should be of crucial importance to achieve this result.

the LAGEOS-type spacecraft in critical supplementary orbits are the most suitable and effective probes to detect the Lense– Thirring effect, with the best possible accuracy level, in the near future, provided that the orbital injection errors are not too large.

, by using a pair of LAGEOs in supplementary orbit configuration, it should be feasible to measure the Lense– Thirring effect in the gravitational field of a rotating, spherical Earth with an accuracy level better than 2% in the next 6 years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a CSOC pair of LAGEOs would be capable of yielding the most stringent tests of the Lense-Thiring effect to date.

the use of two LAGEOS-type spacecraft in supplementary orbits would allow us to measure the Lense– Thirring effect to a much higher accuracy than the present-day best result of 19% (i.e. 3.5 × 10−15 s2) obtained from LAGEOS and LAGEOS II.

, if the Lense– Thirring effect is to be measured with an accuracy level less than 1% with a single pair of LAGEOs, it would be mandatory to launch a new satellite pair in a supplementary orbit configuration.
